source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Thomas Kuhn entry) on Kuhn (1962) The Structure of Scientific Revolutions
finding: Kuhn's cycle: normal science is puzzle-solving inside a shared framework (the disciplinary matrix). Anomalies are first ignored or explained away. Only a build-up of anomalies that undermine the practice causes a crisis. A revolution then revises the matrix. No rule compels the choice of the new framework, and the new one may lose some old explanations (Kuhn-loss).
numbers: Page cites: puzzle-solving pp.35-42; crisis pp.66-76; Kuhn-loss pp.99-100; Lavoisier/Priestley 'transformation of vision' p.118 (1962/1970 edition).
quote: Lavoisier saw oxygen where Priestley saw dephlogisticated air
limits: Entry itself calls the oxygen example somewhat stretched. Kuhn gives no quantitative threshold for when anomalies become a crisis.
agent_relevance: Gives the impasse trigger a shape: do not reframe on the first failed check (anomalies are normal); reframe when failures accumulate and resist the current frame. Supports G1 (doubt only on a signal) and a counted-failure threshold for S6.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Thomas Kuhn entry) on Gestalt switch and Bruner-Postman
finding: Kuhn compared a change of paradigm to a Gestalt switch (duck-rabbit) and drew on Bruner and Postman (1949) for theory-dependent observation. The entry says Kuhn was unsure if the Gestalt idea was only an analogy or a general fact about the mind. The entry does not describe the card experiment itself.
numbers: Bruner and Postman 1949 is mentioned only by date; no figures on the page.
limits: Page gives no card-experiment numbers. The real experiment data are in a07 (not opened).
agent_relevance: A frame can make an anomaly invisible. For the agent, the failing output must be shown to a fresh restatement (O8) because the same frame will keep misreading it.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Incommensurability entry)
finding: Kuhn (1962) said rival paradigms lack a common measure, so partisans only partly communicate. After 1987 he split the idea into taxonomic incommensurability (the no-overlap principle: kind terms cannot cross-classify unless species-to-genus) and methodological incommensurability. He denied that this means incomparable or irrational theory choice. Feyerabend's 1962 version was 'deductively disjoint' theories through meaning variance.
numbers: Dates: Kuhn 1962 (p.150 'different worlds'); breakthroughs from 1987; Feyerabend 1962; Kuhn died 1996. Kuhn 2000 [1991] says incommensurability is 'far from being the threat to rational evaluation of truth claims'.
quote: the proponents of competing paradigms practice their trades in different worlds
limits: Philosophical account, no empirical test. Kuhn could not 'explicate further' the different-worlds claim.
agent_relevance: For the agent: a reframe may change the category scheme (taxonomy), not only the answer. A restated problem should be tested by running, not by arguing that old and new views are comparable in words (G10).

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Scientific Revolutions entry)
finding: Describes paradigm, normal science, anomaly, crisis, revolution, incommensurability and Kuhn loss. Adds history of the word: Condorcet and Lavoisier himself called the chemical change a revolution; Butterfield called it the 'postponed revolution'. Cohen proposed four historical tests for calling an episode a revolution. Later Kuhn moved to 'synchronic' revolutions like speciation.
numbers: Du Chatelet 1740 predates French use; Kuhn moved the quantum revolution start from Planck 1900 to Einstein and Ehrenfest 1905; Copernicus unnoticed by most for about 50 years. Only first 100k of 156k characters read.
limits: Read the first 100,000 characters only. No Thagard ECHO or psychology experiments in the part read.
agent_relevance: Warns that revolutions are labelled after the fact (selection bias, like case studies in HPS). Do not tune the impasse detector on famous successes alone.

source: Wikipedia, The Structure of Scientific Revolutions
finding: Lists the six stages (pre-paradigm, normal science, anomalies, crisis, revolution, post-revolution) and the main criticisms: Popper and Lakatos (1965 Bedford College symposium, 1970 volume), Feyerabend, Toulmin (revision is more frequent and less dramatic), Hanson (circular, unfalsifiable), Kordig (incommensurability too radical, observations are shared), Davidson 1973 (incommensurable schemes incoherent).
numbers: 264 pages in 1962; second edition 1970; over 1 million copies; 16 languages; Copernicus used about as many epicycles as Ptolemy (Koestler count 48 vs 40); Clairaut 1750 explained lunar precession after about 60 years of failed attempts.
limits: Secondary encyclopedia page; the first 100,000 of 147,000 characters read. Epicycle count is from a footnote to Koestler.
agent_relevance: Clairaut's 60-year anomaly that finally yielded to the old theory shows an anomaly may need a patch, not a revolution. The agent should try a cheap repair (S5) before a full reframe (O8), consistent with escalation ordering in the schema.

source: Wikipedia, Phlogiston theory
finding: Oxygen case timeline: Becher's terra pinguis 1667; Stahl named phlogiston 1703; Stahl never explained mass gain when tin and lead burn. Defenders handled the weight anomaly by auxiliary patches: Boyle's negative mass idea, Guyton de Morveau's 'lighter than air'. An Archimedes-principle analysis of magnesium and its oxide showed buoyancy alone could not explain the gain. Lavoisier used weighed closed vessels in the 1770s. Macquer kept rewording the theory while reportedly thinking it doomed.
numbers: Dates: 1667, 1697, 1703, 1723; oxygen identified about 1771, named 1777; nitrogen 1772 (Rutherford); Giobert prize 1792.
limits: Encyclopedia page. It does not give Lavoisier's actual weighings or Kuhn's reading.
agent_relevance: Textbook pattern of patching an anomaly with ad hoc add-ons. A detector for S6 can count patches that explain only the failing case and fail a held-out case (G3). A closed, weighed, held-out test was what broke the deadlock.

source: Bruner and Postman (1949) On the perception of incongruity: a paradigm. Journal of Personality 18:206-223
finding: Subjects saw playing cards briefly, with some anomalous ones (a red six of spades). Anomalous cards needed longer exposure to be named, and subjects first reported them as normal cards (dominance reaction), then showed hesitation and distress. This is the experiment Kuhn used for 'anomaly appears only against a background of expectation'.
numbers: From memory, not read this session: about 28 subjects; ascending exposure series starting near 10 ms. Treat figures as unverified.
limits: Small sample, old methods. Not opened; no citation-quality numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: First reaction to an anomaly is to assimilate it to the expected category. The agent's first fix will usually read a failing output as the usual kind of error, so S6 should force a look at the raw output.

source: Thagard (2002 encyclopedia entry) Conceptual Change, in Encyclopedia of Cognitive Science (offprint conc.change.pdf)
finding: Gives the compact version of anomaly, crisis and revolution with the phlogiston example (objects gain weight in combustion), and says revolutions reclassify concepts (Copernicus: earth becomes a planet; Darwin; computation). Thagard argues that conceptual change does not block rational choice: the main mechanism for large-scale change is explanatory coherence, plus conceptual combination and analogy to build the new system.
numbers: US high-school graduate knows about 60,000 root words, so better than 10 words learned per day; Carey: concepts 'alive' and 'animal' reorganise between ages 4 and 10; first-graders often hold a 'two earths' model.
quote: scientists adopt a new theory along with its conceptual system because it provides a better explanation of the evidence
limits: Intermediate review. Admits evidence is thin that children's change resembles scientists' change; children's knowledge may be fragmented.
agent_relevance: Gives O8 two parts: (1) build the new frame by combination or analogy; (2) choose between old and new frames by explanatory coverage of the evidence, which code can count (S7).

source: Thagard (2002) Conceptual Change - Carey 1985 and Keil 1989 child studies, as reported
finding: Carey (1985): many 4-year-olds cannot name non-living things and treat tables and clocks as alive because they have motion; by 10 most children have the adult concept of living thing; children under 7 often do not count people and insects as animals. Keil (1989): older children say a pear covered in apple skin is still a pear, but no such shift for artefacts like cup and nail, so the change is domain-specific.
numbers: Age band 4 to 10 (Carey); under 7 (animal concept). No sample sizes given in the review.
limits: Second-hand summary; sample sizes not given. Original books not opened.
agent_relevance: Concepts can change shape in one domain and not another; an agent that updates its frame for one problem class should not assume it carries over to another.

source: Thagard (2002) Conceptual Change - Vosniadou and Brewer (1992) earth models, Chi (1992) ontological shift, as reported
finding: Vosniadou and Brewer found children merge the taught round earth with the observed flat earth into synthetic models: two earths (flat one we live on, round one in the sky), or a sphere with people living inside. Chi (1992) argues physics is hard because naive students class force, light, heat and current as material substances while physics needs them as events or fields (a change across ontological categories).
numbers: Review gives no counts. (Original: Cognitive Psychology 24:535-585, not opened here.)
limits: Second-hand; original sample sizes not read.
agent_relevance: Shows how a learner protects the old frame: bolt the new fact onto the old structure. An agent given a correction in context may do the same (a patch, not a reframe); O8 should restate the problem without the old frame in view.

source: Posner, Strike, Hewson and Gertzog (1982) Accommodation of a scientific conception. Science Education 66:211-227
finding: Conceptual-change model with four conditions for a student to give up an old conception: dissatisfaction with it, the new one is intelligible, plausible, and fruitful. Built on Kuhn (assimilation vs accommodation, borrowed from Piaget).
numbers: No empirical figures; a theoretical model. Not opened this session (publisher page returned 403).
limits: Later critics (Pintrich et al. 1993; Vosniadou; diSessa) say it is too rational and ignores motivation and emotion.
agent_relevance: Gives a four-part gate for accepting a new frame: dissatisfaction (a failing check), intelligible (restatement works), plausible (consistent with the rest), fruitful (predicts a new, testable case). Maps to S6 to S8.

source: Chinn and Brewer (1993) The role of anomalous data in knowledge acquisition. Review of Educational Research 63:1-49
finding: Reviewed the ways people respond to anomalous data and sorted them into seven: ignore, reject, exclude as outside the theory's scope, hold in abeyance, reinterpret, make a peripheral theory change, or change the theory. Only the last is full conceptual change.
numbers: Seven response types (from memory of the taxonomy; paper not opened, publisher blocked).
limits: Taxonomy built from cases and classroom studies; later tests (Chinn and Brewer 1998) not opened here.
agent_relevance: Directly usable as an error taxonomy for the impasse detector: the agent's own non-reframe behaviors are ignore, reject output as flaky, scope-exclude, defer, reinterpret the check, patch locally. Code can detect these from the trace.

source: Festinger, Riecken and Schachter (1956) When Prophecy Fails, as reported on Wikipedia Conceptual change
finding: Observers joined a group that expected the world to end on 21 December 1954. After the prediction failed, most believers kept their framework. Used on the page as an example of resisting disconfirming data.
numbers: Prophecy date 21 December 1954. No participant counts on the page.
limits: Secondary page. The original study is a participant-observation of one small group, and the claim that belief strengthened in all members is contested.
agent_relevance: A failed prediction does not by itself cause revision. The agent needs the program, not the model, to register the failure and force the change (G2).

source: Wikipedia, Conceptual change (frameworks section)
finding: Names the main rival accounts: Chi (ontological shift, many naive concepts wrongly in 'matter' not 'process'); Vosniadou (framework theory with entrenched presuppositions); diSessa (knowledge in pieces, change as reorganisation of many small resources, diSessa 1993 Cognition and Instruction 10:105-225); Hartelt and Martens (2024) on self-assessment and metaconceptual knowledge helping students inhibit intuitive conceptions.
numbers: Citations only; no effect sizes on the page. Hartelt and Martens 2024, J Res Sci Teach 61(5):1134-1180.
limits: No statistics on the page; competing accounts not adjudicated.
agent_relevance: Competing accounts differ on whether the old frame is replaced (Chi, Posner) or kept and suppressed (Vosniadou, Hartelt). For an LLM, the old frame stays in the weights, so the second view fits: the scaffold must inhibit it, not delete it.

source: Thagard and Verbeurgt (1998) Coherence as constraint satisfaction. Cognitive Science 22:1-24
finding: Defines coherence as accepting or rejecting elements to maximise satisfied positive and negative constraints. Compares five algorithms: exhaustive, incremental, connectionist, greedy, semidefinite programming. ECHO (explanatory coherence, the model Thagard applied to the chemical revolution) is a connectionist instance.
numbers: Exhaustive search over 100 propositions needs 2^100 = 1,267,650,600,228,229,401,496,703,205,376 solutions. ECHO used on more than a dozen cases (some with more than 150 propositions); fewer than 200 update cycles settle every ECHO net tried. SDP gives at least 0.878 of the optimum. Greedy gives the same result as the connectionist algorithm on tested examples, with random tie-breaks.
limits: Theory and small worked cases, not a human-subject test. Authors note the greedy algorithm is less psychologically plausible.
agent_relevance: Gives a cheap code-side selector for S7: treat hypotheses and evidence as nodes with support and conflict links and run the greedy flip search. No model judging needed (G5).

source: Thagard (2014) Explanatory identities and conceptual change. Science & Education 23:1531-1548
finding: Uses the history of fire, air, water, heat and others to show conceptual change by reclassification ('branch jumping'; Chi calls it categorical shift). Air was thought an element; in the 1780s Scheele, Priestley, Cavendish, Lavoisier showed a mixture. Cavendish read the parts as phlogisticated and dephlogisticated air, and only Lavoisier reinterpreted them as nitrogen and oxygen. Fire went from element to a rapid-oxidation process.
numbers: Dates: air decomposed in the 1780s; Dalton's atoms after 1800; Cavendish and Priestley were phlogiston adherents who still found the data.
limits: Historical narrative by a philosopher; not an experiment. Attribution of discovery is contested.
agent_relevance: The discoverers had the data but read it in the old frame. Same evidence, different frame. This is the case for O8: restate the problem with the old category labels removed and see whether the same output reads differently.

source: Thagard (2006/2008) Conceptual change in the history of science: life, mind, and disease
finding: Argues conceptual change in science moved from theological to qualitative to mechanistic explanations. Three generalisations: concepts move from simple properties to complex relations; conceptual change is theory change; conceptual change is often emotional as well as cognitive. Resistance has cognitive causes (hard to see mechanistic superiority) and emotional causes (the personal implications).
numbers: Examples only; the modern concept of fire is rapid oxidation. Draft dated 9 November 2006.
limits: Interpretive; an emotional-resistance claim is hard to carry to a language model.
agent_relevance: For an LLM, 'emotional' resistance becomes a strong prior from training text. Plain framing still matters: a reframed prompt that drops the familiar story may remove the pull of the common answer.

source: Wu, Qiu, Ross, Akyurek et al. (2023/2024) Reasoning or Reciting? Counterfactual tasks. arXiv 2307.02477
finding: Eleven tasks, each in a default form and a counterfactual form where the default assumption is changed (base-9 arithmetic, 1-based indexing, altered guitar tuning, subject-verb-object order, chess rules). GPT-4 and other models do above chance on the counterfactual versions but fall substantially and consistently below the default versions.
numbers: 11 tasks; models include GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude, PaLM-2; arithmetic is better in base 8 and 16 than in the closer but rarer base 9 and 11; performance gap shrinks for common counterfactuals; default and counterfactual accuracy correlate across variants; 0-shot chain of thought helps in most cases, but hurts PaLM-2 base-10 and base-16 addition and GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 default chord playing.
quote: nontrivial performance on the counterfactual variants, but nevertheless find that performance substantially and consistently degrades
limits: Test is about changing a stated rule, not about revising a belief after anomaly. Exact per-task percentages not recorded here (from figures).
agent_relevance: An LLM is locked to default world assumptions. A reframe that changes the assumed rule (O8) will cost accuracy unless the new world is restated explicitly; do not expect a free switch. CoT is not a cure.

source: Wilie, Cahyawijaya, Ishii, He, Fung (2024) Belief Revision: the adaptability of LLM reasoning (Belief-R). arXiv 2406.19764
finding: Delta-reasoning tests: after a first inference, a new premise may or may not overturn it. Basic logic is good (models over 6B get at least 75%; instruction-tuned from 2.7B get at least 90%). But on belief update most models are near zero. Models that update more do worse at maintaining beliefs when no update is needed.
numbers: About 30 models. Belief-update accuracy (BU) / belief-maintain (BM) / combined BREU, direct prompting: Llama-3 70B 10.99 / 92.09 / 51.54; Mixtral 8x22B 35.38 / 36.57 / 35.98; Command R+ 12.10 / 80.45 / 46.28. Best BREU about 50% (at most 50%). Non-API open models are near 0% BU.
limits: Logic-based updates (modus ponens, modus tollens), not full anomaly-driven change. The abstract concept (mental-state) subset is harder. Table rows for some closed models were hard to read, so only labelled rows are recorded.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that an LLM will keep its first conclusion when a new fact should overturn it, but also that forced doubt breaks correct answers. Supports G1: update only on a code-detected signal.

source: Wilie et al. (2024) Belief-R - effect of prompting and distractors
finding: Chain of thought does not significantly improve belief revision; plan-and-solve adds only about 1 point of BREU. Models do worse on modus tollens updates than modus ponens. A third irrelevant premise lowers accuracy on cases needing no change, so logic is not robust to distractors.
numbers: 378 matched queries used for the distractor comparison. Examples: Claude-3 Haiku BU 13.69, BM 75.67, BREU 44.68 (direct); CoT BU 14.71, BM 77.76. Plan-and-solve gain at most about 1 point BREU.
limits: Prompt effects vary by model; some prompts help one model and hurt another (Table A1). Single benchmark.
agent_relevance: Asking the model to think harder or step by step does not make it revise. Revision must be triggered and checked by code (G2, G11).

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld: a virtual environment for automated scientific discovery agents. arXiv 2406.06769
finding: 120 tasks over 8 topics at 3 difficulty levels, requiring hypothesis, experiment, analysis and action. Some tasks include an anomaly-spotting step (for example, a species that differs from the others). Strong baseline agents (ReAct, Plan-and-Execute, Hypothesizer) mostly fail on end-to-end discovery.
numbers: Best agent (ReAct) completed 38% of easy tasks and 18% of challenge tasks; best at explanatory knowledge (Hypothesizer) found 34% of gold knowledge on easy tasks and 8% on challenge tasks; unit-test tasks (single skills) show completion about 60% or more. Agent tables use GPT-4o, 5 seeds per cell.
limits: Simulated text world; tasks are scored on completion and gold knowledge, not on frame change as such. 24 tasks used for agent tables.
agent_relevance: Shows agents can do component skills but cannot chain them to a new explanation. The step missing is the one Kuhn names: noticing that the working frame fails and moving to another.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld - human scientists
finding: Human scientists (MSc or PhD, recruited on Upwork) did far better than agents on the same tasks. When stuck, they sometimes brute-forced answers without gaining the explanatory knowledge.
numbers: 16 tasks; up to 11 humans per task; average completion 66%; 11 of 16 tasks above 60% completion; average knowledge score 55%.
limits: Small human group; humans had more time and different expertise per task.
agent_relevance: A realistic human reference for 'explanatory discovery': about 55%. Our scaffold's S6 reframes should be judged on knowledge discovered, not on completion that brute force can reach.

source: Agarwal, Majumder et al. (2025) AutoDiscovery: open-ended scientific discovery via Bayesian surprise. arXiv 2507.00310
finding: Treats an anomaly as a measurable belief shift: sample the LLM's belief in a hypothesis before and after seeing experiment results, fit Beta distributions, and define surprise as a flip in leaning (supported to unsupported). Uses MCTS with progressive widening to search nested hypotheses, with surprise as reward.
numbers: 21 datasets; 5 to 29% more LLM-surprising discoveries than strong search baselines at a fixed budget of 500; GPT-4o as discovery agent; prior and posterior estimated as Beta(1+k, 1+n-k) from n samples.
limits: Surprise is judged by the same family of LLM; the human check (a24) tests this.
agent_relevance: A ready code-checkable anomaly detector for S6: compare the model's prior belief (before seeing output) to its posterior (after) and fire only on a leaning flip. Costs n extra samples per check.

source: Agarwal et al. (2025) AutoDiscovery - human evaluation
finding: Experts rated hypotheses found by different rewards. Bayesian surprise matched human surprise far better than asking the LLM directly whether a result is surprising, interesting or useful.
numbers: 1,620 hypotheses pooled from 4 datasets, 3 STEM MS/PhD annotators each; human surprisal 0.67 for Bayesian surprise (95% CI 0.63 to 0.71, bootstrap 10,000) vs 0.11 for direct LLM surprisal overall; the paper says the next best reward is lower by 0.46; by familiarity: low 0.64, medium 0.66, high 0.62.
limits: Four datasets in the human study; annotator agreement for the other rewards was low (about 0.13 to 0.18).
agent_relevance: Asking the model 'is this surprising?' is near-useless; measuring its belief shift is not. Supports G5 and G8: measure, do not ask.

source: Gandhi, Li, Goodman et al. (2025) BoxingGym: benchmarking automated experimental design and model discovery. arXiv 2501.01540
finding: 10 environments, each a generative model the agent can probe. Measures experiment quality (expected information gain) and theory quality (how well a second agent predicts from the first agent's explanation). All LLMs struggle at both, and larger models beat smaller ones (32B over 7B).
numbers: 6 LLMs incl. GPT-4o and Claude-3.7-Sonnet; 5 runs per cell; strong in population growth and death process (negative standardised error means data helped); weak on hyperbolic discounting even after experiments; prior information helps on some tasks.
limits: Models are mostly smooth statistical worlds; no paradigm change as such. NeurIPS 2025 workshop version.
agent_relevance: Theory revision from data is weak and domain-dependent. Our scaffold should expect no free gain from 'revise the theory' prompts, and should measure by prediction on held-out probes (G3).

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) BoxingGym - Box's Apprentice and explanation transfer
finding: Giving the LLM a tool to propose and fit explicit statistical models does not reliably beat the plain LLM; it favours overly simple forms (linear fits for nonlinear processes). Explanations written by a scientist agent help a novice agent less than the scientist's own experiments, and help little in complex domains such as moral judgment.
numbers: GPT-4o with and without Box's Apprentice, 5 runs; GPT-4o lowest EIG regret across several environments; novice agents worse than scientists who experimented directly.
limits: Results are averaged over environments; per-environment values are in the paper's tables.
agent_relevance: A model's account of a new frame loses information when passed on. In handing a reframed problem between steps, pass the raw failing output and held-out probes as well as the explanation.

source: Guzzetti et al. and refutation-text research (not opened); Kuhn-style anomaly confrontation in teaching
finding: Meta-analysis of conceptual-change teaching reports that refutation text, which names the misconception and then refutes it, tends to beat plain expository text. Recorded only as a pointer for the later angle on replications; details were not read.
numbers: Not read; no figures recorded.
limits: Not opened; reference details are from memory and may be wrong. Needs checking in a later pass.
agent_relevance: Refutation format (state the common wrong frame, then show why it fails) is a candidate wording for the O8 restatement prompt. Needs a test at equal tokens (G7).

source: Thagard (1989) Explanatory coherence, Behavioral and Brain Sciences 12:435-502; Thagard (1992) Conceptual Revolutions, Princeton
finding: Original ECHO paper and book: a connectionist program with units for hypotheses and evidence, excitatory links for explanation and inhibitory links for contradiction. Applied to the chemical revolution (Lavoisier vs phlogiston), Copernicus, Darwin and Newton. Reported that ECHO prefers the oxygen theory when given Lavoisier's evidence. The offprint link on the author's site returned an empty file, so this was not read.
numbers: Not read directly. The 1998 paper (a15) says ECHO has been run on more than a dozen cases with fewer than 200 cycles to settle.
limits: Input propositions are encoded by hand, so the answer depends on the coder's choices. Later critics (Glymour 1992) say a simpler calculation could replace it.
agent_relevance: A tested, tiny model of frame choice that code could run. The caveat on hand-encoded input applies: a model-written graph would add the same noise.

source: Kuhn-vs-psychology link: Thagard (2002) on children and scientists - open questions
finding: The review says that whether children's conceptual change matches scientists' change is not settled. Scientists compare the explanatory coherence of two theories in a systematic way; children's change may be piecemeal, gradual build-up of new concepts and disuse of old ones, not dramatic replacement.
numbers: None.
limits: Opinion in a review; the knowledge-in-pieces versus theory debate remains open.
agent_relevance: Two possible shapes for LLM change: jump (reframe) or drift (gradual). Our design choice [D] of a discrete reframe operator is a bet on the jump view; test it against stepwise repair at equal tokens.

source: Gopnik and Meltzoff (1997) Words, Thoughts and Theories, as reported by Thagard (2002)
finding: Theory theory: infants' development is like scientists' theory change. Infants are said to start with 3D objects, have coherent movement knowledge by about 6 months, understand hidden objects around 9 months, and represent invisible movement at about 18 months, each step described as a theory change with some incommensurability.
numbers: Ages 6, 9 and 18 months as stated in the review.
limits: Thagard says evidence is limited that infant change is the same kind of process as scientists' change.
agent_relevance: Weak support only. Useful as a reminder that stage models of change are contested; do not hard-code a stage ladder for the agent.
